title: Three kinds of dukkha
hookLine: plain pain, the pain of change, and the unease built into all made things (SN 45.165)

lines: MONDAY: A FINGER IN A DRAWER.
cards: Three moments from one ordinary week. On Monday you slam your finger in a drawer, and for ten seconds the whole world is your finger.
On Friday it's the last evening of a wonderful trip, the sun going down over the water, and right in the middle of the happiness there's a small sinking feeling, because tomorrow it ends.
On Sunday afternoon, with nothing at all wrong, there's a faint restlessness you can't name. All three are dukkha. But they aren't the same kind.

teach.b: A tiny sutta sorts them, number one hundred sixty-five in the book on the path in the Connected Discourses. The Buddha says there are three kinds of dukkha.

The first is plain pain: the finger in the drawer, the headache, the grief. Nobody needs this one explained. The second is dukkha as change, and it's the strange one, because it lives inside pleasant things.

The trip is lovely, and because it's lovely its ending hurts. Every good thing comes with its end built in. The commentaries count pleasant feeling here: not because pleasure is bad, but because it doesn't stay.
The third is harder to spot: the dukkha of formations, of all conditioned things.

Everything made out of parts, depending on other things, is unstable: your body, your plans, your mood, the economy. On this reading, even a quiet Sunday with nothing wrong rests on ground that isn't solid.
That background unease is the third kind. The sutta itself is very short; the full explanations come from the commentaries, and teachers draw the lines between the three a little differently.

teach.h: THE PATH IS FOR UNDERSTANDING THEM.
teach.b: Why sort them? If all you know is the first kind, you'll think dukkha is only bad luck. The second explains why getting what you wanted didn't settle you.
And the sutta's last sentence ties it to the path: the eightfold path, the Buddha says, is to be developed for fully understanding these three.

how: Buddhist teachers often introduce the three kinds of dukkha when explaining the first truth, and meditators are taught to notice in practice how pleasant feeling, too, changes and passes.

o: the sadness that follows a big loss
the special hardship of monks and nuns
pain, change, and the unease of made things

games.q: match each moment to its kind of dukkha.
p: a finger slammed in a drawer
the last evening of a trip

s: the second kind of dukkha lives inside pleasant things
because pleasant things change, their ending is built in.
the third kind only comes to people who are depressed
it's the unease built into all conditioned things, for everyone.
the sutta explains each kind at length
it's very short; the long explanations come from the commentaries.

games.q: you finally get the job you wanted. a month later you feel strangely unsettled, though nothing is wrong. which kind of dukkha is it, by today's teaching?
o: the pain of change, and the unease of made things.
none: good news can't be dukkha.
games.why: the sutta's second and third kinds explain it: good things change and end, and everything built from parts is unstable underneath.

practice: Find any plain discomfort in the body right now, a tight shoulder, a sore spot, and name it: pain. Think of something pleasant you're looking forward to, notice any tiny edge of worry that it'll end, and name it: change.
Then feel the whole moment, made of a hundred moving parts, and if there's a faint unease underneath, name it: made things.

wordCard.voice: Dukkhatā. The state of being dukkha: plain pain, the pain of change hidden in pleasant things, and the quiet unease in everything made of parts.

orig.note: Pali dukkhatā: the state of being dukkha; the sutta names three, from pain, from change, and from formations.

carryVoice: Your line: three kinds. Pain, change, and the ground moving under made things. That's day three hundred thirty-five.
